hero.headline: Money matters, made clear.
hero.subheadline: Private financial guidance for people who have never felt at home with finance. No jargon, no pressure, no assumptions. Just a trusted broker who explains every option before you decide.

intro.title: You do not need to understand finance to do well in it.
intro.paragraph1: Most people are never taught how money works. They are handed forms, percentages and acronyms, and told to sign. That is not guidance.
intro.paragraph2: As your broker, my job is to translate. I look at your situation, lay out your choices in everyday language, and compare the real costs of each, so the decision you make is one you actually understand.

steps.title: We talk

steps.title: I do the comparing

steps.title: You decide
steps.description: We go through the plan together. You choose at your own pace, and I stay with you after the paperwork is done.

budget.title: Know where your money goes
budget.intro1: A budget is not a punishment. It is a plan that tells your money where to go, so you are never left wondering where it went.
budget.intro2: A common starting point is to divide take-home pay into needs, wants and savings. Treat it as a guide, not a rule. Your city, your family and your goals decide your real numbers.

tips.title: Know your number
tips.text: Start with what actually reaches your account each month.

tips.title: Pay yourself first
tips.text: Move savings out on payday, before spending begins.

tips.title: Cover the essentials
tips.text: Housing, food, transport and bills come before everything else.

tips.title: Review monthly
tips.text: Ten minutes a month keeps small leaks from becoming big ones.

budget.other: Everything else: dining out, subscriptions, leisure
budget.result: Left each month for savings and goals
budget.msgNone: Add your monthly income to see your plan.
budget.msgOver: You are spending more than you earn each month. That is common and fixable, and a short conversation is the best place to start.
budget.msgGood: You are at or above the common 20% savings guide. The next question is where that money works hardest for you.
budget.msgLow: You are saving less than the common 20% guide. Small, specific changes usually close the gap more easily than people expect.
budget.fine: An illustration only. Real budgets include irregular costs, debt payments and goals, which we map out together.

leverage.title: The power of credit, used wisely
leverage.intro: Credit is a tool. Used with care, it lets you own something valuable today that cash alone could not buy, and lets that asset work for you while you pay it off. Used carelessly, it works against you. This is called leverage.
leverage.helps: the asset can grow in value or earn income, the payments fit comfortably in your budget, you keep a cash cushion, and the cost of borrowing is lower than what you can reasonably expect the asset to deliver.
leverage.hurts: the borrowing buys something that loses value, payments stretch you thin, or rates rise and you did not plan for it. Leverage magnifies losses just as it magnifies gains.
leverage.closing: My role is to show you both sides before you borrow, and to tell you honestly when the risk is too high.
leverage.example: $50,000 of your own money buys a $250,000 property with a mortgage.
leverage.slider: If the property value changes by
leverage.rowLeveraged: Return on your $50,000 using a mortgage
leverage.rowPlain: Same $50,000 in the same asset, no borrowing
leverage.fine: A simplified illustration. It ignores interest, fees, taxes and other costs, and property values can fall as well as rise. Borrowing to invest in markets carries even higher risk.

insurance.title: Protection for the people who depend on you
insurance.intro: Life insurance pays a sum of money to the people you choose if you pass away. It can replace income your family relies on, help pay off debts such as a mortgage so they can stay in their home, and cover final expenses or a child's education.

rows.label: What it is
rows.term: Coverage for a set number of years, such as 10, 20 or 30.
rows.permanent: Coverage designed to last your whole life, as long as premiums are paid.

rows.label: Extras
rows.permanent: Some policies build a cash value over time.

rows.label: Often suits
rows.term: Families protecting income and debts during the years they depend on you.
rows.permanent: Lifelong needs, such as leaving an inheritance or planning an estate.

more.title: Already covered through work or your lender?

suggestions.label: Term vs amortization
suggestions.question: What is the difference between a term and an amortization?
suggestions.answer: The term is how long your interest rate and conditions last before you renew. The amortization is the total time planned to repay the whole loan, such as 25 years. You usually renew several times during one amortization.

suggestions.label: How much to save?
suggestions.question: How much should I save each month?
suggestions.answer: A common starting point is about 20% of take-home pay, but the right number depends on your goals and expenses. Try the budget tool above, then book a consultation to set a figure that fits you.

suggestions.label: Is life insurance worth it?
suggestions.question: Is life insurance worth it?
suggestions.answer: It is worth considering if someone depends on your income or would inherit debts such as a mortgage. If nobody depends on you, you may need little or none. Term coverage is often the simplest and least costly place to start.

suggestions.label: When is borrowing smart?
suggestions.question: When is borrowing a good idea?
suggestions.answer: Borrowing can make sense when it buys something that can grow in value or earn income, when payments fit comfortably in your budget, and when you keep a cash cushion. It is risky when it stretches your budget or buys things that lose value.
